items.title: Sketching a Line Using Two Points

sections.normalized_html: Sketch the graph of [MATH: y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3.]
sections.readable_text: Sketch the graph of [MATH: y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We need to find two distinct points that lie on our line. Any two points will do!

It is often easiest to pick one of the points to have an [MATH: x]-coordinate of [MATH: x=0.] So, for the first point, we will let the [MATH: x]-coordinate be [MATH: x=0.] Then the [MATH: y]-coordinate is

[MATH: y|= − (1)/(2)x + 3; = − (1)/(2)(0) + 3; = 0 + 3; = 3.]

So, the first point is [MATH: (0,3).]

For the second point, let's choose [MATH: x=4.] Then the [MATH: y]-coordinate is [MATH: y|= − (1)/(2)x + 3; = − (1)/(2)(4) + 3; = − 2 + 3; = 1.]

So, the second point is [MATH: (4,1).]

Finally, we plot those two points on the [MATH: xy]-plane and draw a line through them. This is the graph of [MATH: y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3.]

items.title: Identifying a Line Given a Graph

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following gives the graph of the straight line below?

  1. [MATH: y=2x-1]

  2. [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{2}x-1]

  3. [MATH: 2x-y=1]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following gives the graph of the straight line below?

1. [MATH: y=2x-1]
2. [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{2}x-1]
3. [MATH: 2x-y=1]

[IMG: /graphics/fa1b5bcf9bb45d462296327059765c5e]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's pick two distinct points on the line. For example, we can choose [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] with coordinates [MATH: (0,-1)] and [MATH: (2,3)], respectively.

Now, we substitute the coordinates of both points in our equations. If both points satisfy an equation, then we can conclude that the equation represents the line in the graph. Otherwise, if any point does not satisfy the equation, then we can conclude that the equation does not represent the line in the graph.

  • Equation I: [MATH: y=2x-1.] Substituting the coordinates of [MATH: A(0,-1)] and [MATH: B(2,3),] we obtain [MATH: (− 1)|= 2(0) − 1; − 1|= − 1✓; (3)|= 2(2) − 1; 3|= 3✓] Therefore, [MATH: y=2x-1] is an equation of the line in the graph.

  • Equation II: [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{2}x-1.] Substituting the coordinates of [MATH: A(0,-1)] and [MATH: B(2,3),] we obtain [MATH: (− 1)|= (1)/(2)(0) − 1; − 1|= − 1✓; (3)|= (1)/(2)(2) − 1; 3|= 0×] Therefore, [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{2}x-1] is not an equation of the line in the graph.

  • Equation III: [MATH: 2x-y=1.] Substituting the coordinates of [MATH: A(0,-1)] and [MATH: B(2,3),] we obtain [MATH: 2(0) − (− 1)|= 1; 1|= 1✓; 2(2) − (3)|= 1; 1|= 1✓] Therefore, [MATH: 2x-y=1] is an equation of the line in the graph.

Of the given equations, the only equations that represented the line in the graph were [MATH: y=2x-1] and [MATH: 2x-y=1,] corresponding to answer choices I and III. Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we want to plot the graph of [MATH: y = x + 2.] We can do this by substituting some [MATH: x]-values into the equation, calculating the corresponding [MATH: y]-values, and plotting the [MATH: xy]-pairs.

Content:
We'll start by creating a table of values for [MATH: x] and [MATH: y], including a few values of [MATH: x] to begin with.

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: -5] | [MATH: -4] | [MATH: -3] | [MATH: -2] | [MATH: -1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 5] |
| [MATH: y] | | | | | | | | | | | |

Content:
Using our equation [MATH: y=x+2,] we can calculate the corresponding values for [MATH: y.] So for [MATH: x=-5,] we have

Content:
[MATH: y = -5+2 = {\color{blue}{-3}},]

Content:
and we add this to our table:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: -5] | [MATH: -4] | [MATH: -3] | [MATH: -2] | [MATH: -1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 5] |
| [MATH: y] | [MATH: {\color{blue}{-3}}] | | | | | | | | | | |

We repeat this process to fill in the rest of the table:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: -5] | [MATH: -4] | [MATH: -3] | [MATH: -2] | [MATH: -1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 5] |
| [MATH: y] | [MATH: -3] | [MATH: -2] | [MATH: -1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: 6] | [MATH: 7] |

Content:
Then, we plot these [MATH: (x,y)] pairs on the [MATH: xy]-plane:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/30c247da0789abe45558a73652288f75]

Content:
Finally, connecting the points gives us a straight line.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c5a8a8341fffddd7359b5bdc652fea0f]

This is the graph of [MATH: y = x + 2.]

Item 2 — Example: Plotting a Line Using a Table

Use the table below to plot the graph of [MATH: y=3x-2.]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we fill the table. Given a value of [MATH: x,] we can find the corresponding [MATH: y] by substituting [MATH: x] into the formula [MATH: y=3x-2.]
Therefore,

- if [MATH: x=0] then [MATH: y=3(0)-2=-2,]
- if [MATH: x=1] then [MATH: y=3(1)-2=1,]
- if [MATH: x=2] then [MATH: y=3(2)-2=4,] and
- if [MATH: x=3] then [MATH: y=3(3)-2=7.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: A Line Passing Through Two Points

Content:
The graph of a linear equation will always be a straight line! As we know, any straight line is defined by two points.
Therefore, instead of plotting lots of points, we only need to plot two of them, and then we can draw a straight line through them.

For example, we previously encountered a line that passed through the points [MATH: (0,-2),] [MATH: (1,1),] [MATH: (2,4),] and [MATH: (3,7).] Its graph is shown below:

Item 6 — Example: Sketching a Line Using Two Points

Example Prompt:
Sketch the graph of [MATH: y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We need to find two distinct points that lie on our line. Any two points will do!

It is often easiest to pick one of the points to have an [MATH: x]-coordinate of [MATH: x=0.] So, for the first point, we will let the [MATH: x]-coordinate be [MATH: x=0.] Then the [MATH: y]-coordinate is

[MATH: y|= − (1)/(2)x + 3; = − (1)/(2)(0) + 3; = 0 + 3; = 3.]

So, the first point is [MATH: (0,3).]

For the second point, let's choose [MATH: x=4.] Then the [MATH: y]-coordinate is
[MATH: y|= − (1)/(2)x + 3; = − (1)/(2)(4) + 3; = − 2 + 3; = 1.]

So, the second point is [MATH: (4,1).]

Finally, we plot those two points on the [MATH: xy]-plane and draw a line through them. This is the graph of [MATH: y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3.]

[IMG: /graphics/59583e209f4bf6bf53ab3450bb0b028e]
